Text: $SNDK $MU NAND flash to become the next major supply bottleneck and potentially experience the strongest price increases in 2027. Kumar said one distributor estimated demand at roughly three times available supply. He expects supply and demand to remain out of balance throughout 2027 and potentially into part of 2028. Rising HBM production is also tightening conventional DRAM availability because HBM requires roughly three times the die area, Kumar said. At the same time, agentic AI applications are increasing demand for server DRAM such as DDR5. Kumar expects NAND flash to become the next major supply bottleneck and potentially experience the strongest price increases next year.

Author: mikirduit
Text: $MU beat earnings expectations, but investors barely reacted. Is the AI trade losing momentum—or was strong growth already priced in? The key issue is the source of growth. Micron’s latest quarter benefited more from higher memory prices than shipment growth. That supports profitability, but raises a tougher question: how much can earnings grow when prices stop climbing? Healthy AI demand can coexist with slower earnings growth. New capacity also requires substantial spending before it generates cash. One muted reaction doesn’t prove AI enthusiasm is fading. It does suggest investors may need more than another earnings beat: durable pricing, stronger volumes and cash flow that justifies the valuation. Are you watching headline growth—or how long it can last?

Text: 🎯 Bullseye Analysis: Toshiba's impact on HDD and DRAM/HBM/NAND 🎯 A lot of people in the Bullseye trading room were asking yesterday about my thoughts on the Toshiba HDD deal and its implications for DRAM, NAND, and HBM companies short and long term, so I wanted to share a more detailed breakdown now that I've had time to review everything. The timeline of how this news broke is revealing. The headline hit around 10:30 PM ET on Thursday, yet $STX and $WDC did not move at all until roughly 6:00 AM Friday morning. That delayed reaction shows Mr. Market and the algos were digesting a mid-to-long-term capacity story rather than a sudden shift in near-term fundamentals. There is zero immediate impact to current revenue or earnings estimates, and both $STX and $WDC should keep beating and raising every quarter for the next few years. Looking at HDD mid-to-long term, Toshiba's $380 million commitment aims to double capacity and reach 30% market share by 2030, attempting to shift the HDD duopoly into a triopoly, which is how the DRAM and HBM industry operates today. While Toshiba makes great hardware with its nearline HDD designs, real market impact won't hit until the 2029 to 2030 timeframe given factory ramps, yield optimization, and lengthy hyperscaler qualifications. Until then, $STX and $WDC hold a massive lead in 40TB+ HAMR and ePMR volume, keeping pricing power firmly in their hands. Now on to $MU, $SNDK, and $SKHY. DRAM and NAND will be shielded from a similar surprise supply shock. Building a modern 3D NAND or DRAM fab requires over $10 billion, not a few hundred million. While Chinese production remains the biggest potential threat on paper, strict US export restrictions and lack of access to advanced lithography equipment prevent those companies from flooding Western enterprise channels with cutting-edge memory nodes. Final takeaway: While we could see short-term volatility across all of these names as the market digests capacity news, it's simply too early to say what the true long-term implications will be for $STX and $WDC as Toshiba attempts its multi-year ramp. However, we see DRAM and NAND as much more shielded. With foreign producers bottlenecked by equipment sanctions and major memory OEMs actively reallocating cleanroom space away from standard NAND into high-margin HBM and DDR5 for AI clusters, Enterprise SSD and DRAM supply will stay structurally tight. Consumer demand for PCs and smartphones collapsed, prices fell below production costs, and companies burned billions. The entire industry was forced to cut capital expenditures, shut down production lines, and completely stop building new factory capacity. • The AI Supply Crunch: Just as capacity shrank, the generative AI boom exploded. Cloud hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, AWS) desperately needed High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM3E) to feed their NVIDIA AI chips. Because Micron underinvested in factories during the 2023 crash, they found themselves completely capacity-constrained, shifting from a boring commodity business into an absolute trillion-dollar bottleneck for global technology. • The Hard Financial Proof: Fiscal Q4 2026 results completely destroyed conservative Wall Street models. Micron is aggressively building multi-billion-dollar plants, and if factory capacity outpaces AI demand by late 2028 or 2029, an oversupply wave will cause memory prices to slide. • Why the Demand Can Last: The long-term secular truth is that the more technology advances, the more data is generated, meaning an exponentially larger amount of memory is needed to store it. AI networks, robo-taxis, and robotics are massive data hogs. If a system runs out of advanced memory, the global data highway overflows, slows down, and freezes. We need companies like Micron to prevent this overflow. • The Cannibalization Moat: Building one single gigabit of advanced HBM memory uses up approximately three times the physical silicon wafer capacity required to build standard DRAM. By shifting manufacturing lines to high-margin AI data center contracts, Micron is naturally strangling the supply of regular memory for smartphones, PCs, and automotive fleets, keeping prices high. Text: $MU Title: Why Micron ($MU) is No Longer a Cyclical Stock Let’s address the big question. Wall Street still treats Micron ($MU) as a fragile commodity stock, capping its valuation multiple. Text: $MU Is Micron a Millionaire-Maker Stock After Its 2026 Run? Read full article on The Motley Fool. The AI boom represented a fresh growth opportunity for Micron. But revenue growth truly took off in recent quarters as the agentic AI opportunity emerged. Agentic AI involves AI addressing an issue on behalf of a human and taking various steps to complete tasks. This represents an almost limitless opportunity for memory and storage companies, as these chips are needed on an ongoing basis for AI agents to operate. By comparison, training needs the memory capacity once, as the training is happening. So agentic AI represents a much bigger growth opportunity for memory makers like Micron. Text: SK Hynix’s decision to cancel plans for a U.S. IPO of its Solidigm business could benefit Micron Technology and SanDisk by reducing the risk of additional NAND flash memory capacity entering the market, according to LYNX Equity Strategies. In an October 23 note, analysts led by KC Rajkumar said the IPO would have provided Solidigm with funding to expand U.S. NAND manufacturing capacity, potentially increasing global supply in three or more years and pressuring prices and competing suppliers. The proposed facility could have involved a joint venture with Intel, possibly at Intel’s Ohio campus, where operations might have faced fewer trade restrictions than Solidigm’s existing manufacturing facility in China. LYNX said canceling the IPO removes a potential source of future supply growth, which could support NAND pricing and valuations for Micron and SanDisk.
